greenlist~

An AI watermark, run without its restraint
What you are looking at

When an AI writes text, it can leave a hidden signature. The signature is not in the letters, the spacing, or any invisible character — you could inspect every byte and find nothing. It is hidden in which words got chosen.

It works like this:

  1. At almost every point in a sentence, several words would do. "I poured a cup of ___" — coffee, tea, water. That freedom is the room the signature hides in.
  2. Before each word, a secret key and the previous word are fed into a scrambler that paints every word in the dictionary either green (allowed here) or red (not allowed here). Nobody decides the colours and they mean nothing — they are as patternless as a coin toss, and they are repainted at every single position.
  3. The AI is nudged: when you can, pick a green word. Since about half of all words are green and there is usually a choice, it almost always can — and the sentence reads perfectly normally. You notice nothing.
  4. To check a text, someone holding the key recounts the colours. A human hits green about half the time, by luck. Far more than half means a machine wrote it.

A real watermark depends on that nudge staying gentle. Its entire value is that you cannot feel it. This instrument welds the nudge wide open — same algorithm, no restraint — and forces your words onto the green list until the sentences come apart.

So the output shows two things at once. The colour tells you which list a word is on: green allowed, red forbidden. A box tells you the machine spoke there — it threw out your forbidden word and put a green one in its place. Boxed words are therefore always green, because being green is the whole reason they were chosen.

Which produces the thing worth staring at. The meter on the right is a real detector score. The more thoroughly the text is destroyed, the more confidently it certifies as machine-made. Maximum ruin is maximum proof. Watch the meter climb as the sentence dies — that pairing is the piece.

input 0 words
Type, paste, or load a plain-text file (.txt or .md). Anything you write becomes the material.
key
What is this
The password that colours the dictionary. Fed to the scrambler together with each previous word, it decides which words count as green at every position. Change one character and every colouring in the piece is repainted: same text in, entirely different poem out. There is no correct result — only the one this key produces.
bias0.60
What is this
How often the machine overrules you. When your word lands on the red list, this is the chance it gets swapped for a green one. A working watermark holds this near zero so the change stays invisible — that restraint is the whole reason watermarks work. At 0 your text is untouched. At 1 every forbidden word is replaced. This single dial is the difference between a watermark and this instrument.
cascade0.50
What is this
Whether the machine listens to you or to itself. Each colouring depends on the word before it — but which one? At 0, the word you wrote, so the glitch always argues with your original. At 1, the word it just substituted, so it feeds on its own output and drifts further with every step. At 1.00 the two scores below also agree exactly; see the note under the meter for why.
affinity
What is this
Once a replacement is needed, which green word gets picked. random takes any green word at all — pure noise. shape prefers one of similar length, so the sentence keeps its skeleton while losing its mind. echo draws only on words already in your text, so the passage recombines itself. (Only applies to the pool vocabulary — wordnet and model supply their own candidates.)
gate
What is this
Whether the small words can be taken. all puts every word at risk. content only spares the, of, is, and — grammar's scaffolding stays upright while the meaning walks out from under it. Usually the more unsettling of the two, because the sentence still looks like a sentence.
vocabulary
pool — one fixed word list.
What is this
Where candidate replacements come from before the key filters them. The key always has the final say on which candidate is green — the vocabulary only decides what is on offer.

pool — a fixed word list built into this file. Honest about being a list; makes no attempt at fluency.
wordnet — words sharing an immediate parent in a lexical hierarchy, so coffee offers tea and cocoa. Note the limit: WordNet never reads your sentence, so its offer is the same in every context. Semantic, not predictive.
model — candidates a language model proposed for that exact slot in that exact sentence. Prepared in advance and frozen into this file; a vocabulary belongs to one passage, so editing the text unbinds it. What remains beyond reach either way: a real watermark nudges the model's raw probabilities before it picks a word, and no text interface exposes those.

This file makes no network requests of any kind.
certification z = 0.0 σ
0 1.5σ human 5σ certified 8σ
Paste text to begin
What is this
How far above chance the green count sits, measured in standard deviations. Under 1.5σ reads as human — roughly what luck alone produces. Past 5σ, a detector holding this key would call the text machine-authored.

Two scores are shown because they are computed from different information. This machine can see the word you originally wrote; a detector only ever sees the result. Below cascade 1.00 the two follow different chains of context, so they disagree — and the disagreement can fall either way. The detector's number is the one that matters: it is the verdict attached to the text once it leaves here. At cascade 1.00 the two agree exactly.
What am I looking at
Hover any cell to read the words around it. Click to jump to that word in the text.
Tap any of the three to mute it and see what the others are doing on their own. Muted words stay readable, just greyed.
What is real here. The colouring, the verdict on each of your words, the feedback between one word and the next, and the score — all of it is the genuine keyed green-list mechanism, the same family of scheme used to mark AI-generated text. Nothing is simulated for effect. What has been changed is one number: the restraint. A working watermark keeps the override so rare you could never feel it; here the dial opens all the way.

Which is why every yellow word is worth reading twice. Not a mistake and not random — a place where a key you do not hold decided a word better than the one you chose. The mechanism built to prove a machine wrote something turns out, run hard enough, to be a machine for taking authorship away. And the meter rises the whole time.

Based on the green list / red list watermarking scheme of John Kirchenbauer, Jonas Geiping, Yuxin Wen, Jonathan Katz, Ian Miers and Tom Goldstein — A Watermark for Large Language Models, ICML 2023. The keyed vocabulary partition, the bias added to green tokens, and the z-test used to detect the mark are all theirs; this instrument only removes the restraint.
